title: Kofi Brokeman
localName: Kofi Brokeman — grilled plantain with groundnuts
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: Just-ripe plantain grilled over charcoal and eaten with shelled roasted peanuts, skins still on — a complete meal in itself, inexpensive and filling.
longDesc: The most Ghanaian thing on any roadside: plantain slices grilled over charcoal and handed over with a twist of roasted groundnuts. The plantain must be just ripe, cut on the diagonal into ovals, and the grill rack brushed with oil or lined with non-stick foil to keep it from sticking. Grill until brown and cooked on each side, perhaps five to ten minutes a side. No salt, no spice, nothing else — the sweetness of the plantain against the salt and fat of the peanuts is the whole dish. The name translates, roughly, as Kofi has no money.
ingredients: Just-ripe plantains — no quantity is printed in the source; allow 1 per person
Shelled roasted peanuts with their skins still on — sold ready-roasted, not prepared here
// Do not salt the plantain. See the note.
equipment: Charcoal grill, or a gas grill
Non-stick aluminium foil (alternative to oiling the rack)
steps: Build a fire in a charcoal grill, or fire up a gas grill.
Brush oil on the grill rack to keep the plantain from sticking. Alternatively use non-stick aluminium foil and put the plantain directly on that.
Cut the ends off a just-ripe plantain.
Make a shallow cut just through the peel from end to end on one side, peel it, and remove any stringy fibres.
Cut the plantain on the diagonal, making ovals on the cut ends, to make several slices.
Grill the plantain pieces until they are brown and cooked on each side — perhaps 5 to 10 minutes per side.
Monitor them carefully to prevent burning.
Serve with shelled roasted peanuts, skins still on.
chefTips: Just-ripe is the whole thing. Green plantain will not caramelise and over-ripe collapses through the bars.
Brown and cooked on each side, perhaps five to ten minutes a side. The wide range is honest — it depends entirely on your coals.
Oil the rack or use non-stick foil. Plantain welds itself to a bare grill.
Do not salt it. The peanuts carry the salt, and that contrast is the dish.
Cut on the diagonal for ovals rather than straight across. More surface for the grill and it is how it is sold.
The groundnuts come with their skins on and are bought ready-roasted. The source gives no recipe for them and none is needed.
A complete meal in itself, inexpensive and filling, in her own words. Eat it with your fingers from the paper.
commonMistakes: Cutting straight across instead of on the diagonal.
sources: Adapted from 'Recipe #86: "Kofi Brokeman" (grilled plantain slices)', within the post 'On Ghana's "Kofi Brokeman," "shandies" and Charcoal Grilled Chicken', betumiblog.blogspot.com, Friday 15 July 2011. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 12:41 PM', timestamped 2011-07-15T12:41:00-05:00. Confirmed across three fetches (TWO-PASS).

A SUBSTANTIAL SOURCING CAVEAT, stated plainly: THERE IS NO FORMATTED INGREDIENT LIST AND NO QUANTITY FOR ANYTHING. No number of plantains, no weight, no amount of oil, no amount of groundnuts. Both verbatim passes confirmed the absence. The 'allow 1 per person' in the ingredient line is labelled as an allowance, not as a source figure, and the four servings is editorial.

WHY IT PUBLISHES DESPITE THAT: the technique is fully specified, the doneness cue is observable and printed, and the dish is one where quantity is genuinely a matter of appetite — you grill as many plantains as there are people. Nothing has been invented; the gap is named.

Method as printed, verbatim: 'build a fire in a charcoal grill (or fire up your gas grill), and be sure to brush oil on the grill rack to keep the plantain from sticking. Alternatively, use some "no stick" aluminum foil and put the plantain directly on that.' Preparation: 'cut the ends off, make a shallow cut just through the peel from end to end on one side, peel it and remove any stringy fibers, then cut the plantain on the diagonal (making ovals on the cut ends) to make several slices.'

THE DONENESS CUE, verbatim: 'Grill the plantain pieces until they are brown and cooked on each side (perhaps 5-10 minutes per side).' Observable colour cue with a hedged time. NO TEMPERATURE is printed — it is charcoal.

'DO NOT SALT' and 'monitor carefully to prevent burning' are SINGLE-PASS, from one pass only and not reproduced in the verbatim passes. The no-salt instruction is consistent with Ghanaian street practice but is marked unconfirmed rather than presented as source text.

ON THE GROUNDNUTS: integral to the street dish but SOLD READY-ROASTED and not prepared in the recipe, which is why #86 covers only the plantain. The one specific characteristic printed is worth keeping: the peanuts come 'with their skins still on'. For a made-from-scratch spiced groundnut snack, see GHA108.

THE CULTURAL DESCRIPTION, quoted: Kofi Brokeman is roadside vendor food consisting of 'grilled slices' of just-ripe plantains sold 'along with small paper- or plastic-wrapped packages of shelled roasted peanuts with their skins still on'. And: 'a complete meal in itself, it is inexpensive and filling'. On the name: '(in other words, Kofi has no money)'.

TWO COMPANION RECIPES IN THE SAME POST ARE NOT PUBLISHED, and the reasons are recorded. RECIPE #87, SHANDY: it carries NO NUMERIC QUANTITIES AT ALL — 'part lager beer and part ginger ale (or other soft drink or citrus drink) in whatever proportion you desire', against a commentary figure of 'roughly equal quantities'. With no measures of any kind it is a description rather than a recipe. Worth recording that it uses commercially fermented lager as a bought ingredient and ferments nothing, that no palm wine appears anywhere in the post, and that the author calls it 'perhaps most popular with women in Ghana'; named Ghanaian beers 'Star or Club' are SINGLE-PASS.

RECIPE #88, GHANA-STYLE CHARCOAL GRILLED CHICKEN, is not published for a SAFETY reason and it is named rather than glossed. Its marinade is fully quantified and TWO-PASS — 1 peeled onion or several shallots in large chunks; a fresh chilli, seeded; 2 good-sized garlic cloves; a couple of tablespoons of water, just enough to blend; 1 tsp salt; 1/2 to 1 tsp dried ground red pepper; 1 tbsp tomato paste (optional); 1/4 cup vegetable oil; 2 tsp poultry seasoning; 1 chicken in pieces — blended to a paste, marinated 'for a couple of hours (in the refrigerator)' or 'at least half an hour'. BUT THE SOURCE PRINTS NO GRILLING TIME, NO TEMPERATURE AND NO DONENESS CUE OF ANY KIND for the chicken: no internal temperature, no colour, no juices-running-clear. Its only cooking instruction is 'Baste the chicken with the excess marinade as it cooks, turning it from time to time' — and that basting liquid has been in contact with raw chicken, with no instruction to stop basting before the end of cooking. Publishing a chicken recipe with no doneness cue is not acceptable in this collection, and no conventional figure has been supplied to patch it. The marinade is recorded here for anyone who wants it with their own cooking judgement.

A NOTE ON THE COLLECTION'S OTHER PLANTAIN ENTRIES, so this one is not read as a duplicate: kelewele is diced, spiced and deep-fried (GHA049, GHA050); tatale is mashed over-ripe plantain fried as a pancake (GHA058); krakro is its grated cousin (GHA048). Kofi Brokeman is the only one that is plain charcoal-grilled slices with nothing on them.
NO YIELD is printed on any of the three recipes in the post.
storage: Eat at once. Grilled plantain goes leathery within the hour.
reheating: Briefly on a hot grill. It will not be as good.
healthBenefits: Plantain is high in resistant starch, potassium, vitamin A and vitamin B6.
Peanuts complete the amino acid profile the plantain lacks, making the pair a complete protein.
No added fat beyond what the rack needs, unlike fried plantain.
Vegan, gluten-free and high in fibre.
culturalNote: Kofi Brokeman is the cheapest full meal in Ghana and its name is the joke at its own expense — Kofi is broke, so Kofi is eating plantain and groundnuts, and Kofi is doing fine. Grilled plantain with roasted peanuts is also, by accident of nutrition, a complete protein: the starch and the nut between them supply every amino acid a person needs, which is a good note on which to close a Ghanaian collection.
